issue.issue_text: Whether the review jurisdiction of the Disciplinary Committee of the Bar Council of India (BCI) is wider than the review jurisdiction of a court under Section 114 of the Code of Civil Procedure read with Order XLVII Rule 1.

facts: The Bar Council of India (BCI), while hearing a review petition, took the position that its review jurisdiction is wider than the review jurisdiction of a court under Section 114 and Order XLVII Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC).
Relying on this wider jurisdiction, the BCI allowed a review petition, set aside its previous order, and directed a fresh consideration of the matter.
law: The Supreme Court affirmed the legal principle, citing its previous judgment in *O.N. Mohindroo v. District Judge, Delhi & Anr.*, that the review power of the BCI's Disciplinary Committee is not confined to the narrow parameters laid down in the CPC.
However, the Court established a crucial limitation: this wider power cannot be extended to the extent that the reviewing authority becomes an appellate authority over its own earlier order.
application: The Court found that the BCI had gone beyond the permissible scope of even a liberally construed review power.
The BCI had reviewed its own findings of fact and overturned them based on the same material and arguments that had been presented earlier.
The Court held that by doing so, the BCI was not merely reviewing its order but was impermissibly acting as an appellate authority over its own decision.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the BCI's exercise of its review power in this specific case. It held that while the BCI's review jurisdiction is indeed wider than that of a court under the CPC, it is not unlimited. The BCI cannot use this power to re-evaluate the merits of a case on the same evidence and arguments, as this would amount to acting as an appellate court over its own order, which is beyond the scope of review.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Bar Council of India (BCI) was justified in withdrawing a case to itself from the Disciplinary Committee of the State Bar Council on the ground that the one-year period for disposal under Section 36B of the Advocates Act, 1961 had expired.

facts: The Bar Council of India (BCI) was hearing a review petition concerning a disciplinary matter against an advocate (the respondent).
In its review order, the BCI decided that the respondent had been denied a fair trial because he was not given an opportunity to cross-examine a witness (PW-1).
Based on this finding, the BCI set aside its previous order and decided that a fresh enquiry was needed.
law: Section 36B of the Advocates Act, 1961, provides a one-year time limit for the Disciplinary Committee of a State Bar Council to dispose of a complaint.
application: Instead of sending the case back to the State Bar Council's Disciplinary Committee for the fresh enquiry, the BCI decided to withdraw the case to itself.
The BCI's justification for this withdrawal was its interpretation of Section 36B of the Act.
The BCI reasoned that since the one-year period for disposal had expired, the jurisdiction of the State Bar Council's Disciplinary Committee had come to an end.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the BCI's action. The Court found that the BCI's entire review order, which included the decision to withdraw the case, was an improper and unsustainable exercise of its review powers. By setting aside the BCI's review order in its entirety, the Court invalidated the BCI's decision to withdraw the case and the justification it had provided under Section 36B.

cases.case_name: O.N. Mohindroo v. District Judge, Delhi & Anr.
cases.principle: The powers of review are not circumscribed by the Act. The analogy of the Civil Procedure Code must not be carried too far. Such powers may be exercised in a suitable case for or against an advocate even after the matter has gone through the hands of the Disciplinary Committee at some stage or even through this Court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Even when liberally construed, the review powers of the Bar Council of India's Disciplinary Committee are not unlimited and cannot be exercised in a manner that goes much beyond their intended scope.
obiter: All processes of the court are intended to secure justice, and one such process is the power of review.

If a manifest wrong has been done, it is never too late to undo the wrong, as the limitations placed on civil courts' review powers are absent in the review powers of the Disciplinary Committee under the Advocate’s Act, 1961.
The review powers of the Disciplinary Committee are not circumscribed by the Act, and the analogy of the Civil Procedure Code must not be carried too far.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Bar Council of India (BCI) improperly exercised its review jurisdiction by showing undue indulgence to the respondent-advocate. The Court found that the BCI, under the guise of correcting a 'manifest wrong,' allowed the respondent to take advantage of his own procedural wrongs, effectively re-hearing an appeal on merits on a point it had already considered and rejected. This action went far beyond the permissible scope of review powers, even when liberally construed, and was therefore unsustainable.
legal_tests_applied: Nullus Commodum Capere Potest De Injuria Sua Propria: A legal maxim meaning a party cannot be permitted to take advantage of its own wrong or manipulations to frustrate the legal rights of others.
why_appellant_lost: The BCI showed undue indulgence to the respondent by allowing him to take advantage of his own wrong, in the guise of exercising its review power.
The BCI, in its review order, revisited an issue on the merits that it had already considered and specifically rejected in its original appellate order dated September 10, 2011.
why_respondent_won: The Court held that the BCI had gone 'much beyond the scope of review powers, even when these are liberally construed.'
While acknowledging the principle that a manifest wrong should be undone, the Court found its application by the BCI on the facts of the instant case to be 'clearly unsustainable.'
policy_considerations: The maxim nullus commodum capere potest de injuria sua propria has a clear mandate of law that, a person who by manipulation of a process frustrates the legal rights of others, should not be permitted to take advantage of his wrong or manipulations.
All processes of the court are intended to secure justice and one such process is the power of review.
